eyebrow: Product designer / information architect / solution thinker
heading: From explaining systems to shaping products.
intro: My career began with information: learning unfamiliar technology, finding its underlying logic, and explaining it without losing the important parts. That work gradually moved upstream—from documenting finished systems to questioning, structuring, designing, and prototyping the product itself.
positioning: I am useful when the problem is still unclear, the system has too many moving parts, or a team needs a practical way forward.

I work across product framing, information architecture, UX, interface design, content, and working prototypes. I use code and AI-assisted development to test ideas early—not to decorate a finished answer.

capabilities.title: Frame the problem
capabilities.copy: Separate the real user or business problem from the requested feature. Turn ambiguity into a question the team can act on.

capabilities.title: Map the system
capabilities.copy: Understand actors, information, dependencies, edge cases, and constraints before deciding what the interface should do.

capabilities.title: Design the experience
capabilities.copy: Create flows, content structures, interaction patterns, and visual hierarchy that reduce effort without hiding necessary complexity.

capabilities.title: Make it testable
capabilities.copy: Use prototypes, code, and AI-assisted development to expose weak assumptions and move a useful idea closer to reality.

bridgeHeading: What the job titles do not show.
bridge: Technical communication is often treated as work that begins after the product decisions are made. In practice, doing it well requires product thinking: reconstructing the user’s goal, questioning the sequence, finding missing states, naming concepts, and deciding what should be visible when.

That is the bridge to my product-design work. I did not leave systems thinking behind to become a designer; I brought it with me. The difference is that I now use those skills earlier, while the experience can still be changed.

process.title: Ask what changed
process.copy: Why is this problem important now? Who feels it, and what are they doing today?

process.title: Make the invisible visible
process.copy: Write the model down. Map the actors, decisions, information, constraints, and uncomfortable edge cases.

process.title: Reduce without oversimplifying
process.copy: Remove avoidable work and noise while keeping the detail people need to make a correct decision.

process.title: Build enough to learn
process.copy: A working prototype answers questions that a polished static screen can hide.

process.title: Listen to the working thing
process.copy: Use what breaks, confuses, or slows people down as input for the next version.
